title: CRM Lead Reconciliation: Build Data You Can Trust
excerpt: Learn how to reconcile Meta leads, spreadsheets and CRM records using clear identities, conservative matching, safe updates and verifiable attribution.
body:
An advertising platform reports one enquiry. A spreadsheet contains two similar rows. The CRM has an older contact and a newer deal. Which record should receive the campaign attribution?

The tempting answer is to match the phone number and move on. That can quietly attach the wrong campaign to the wrong enquiry, erase a legitimate repeat request or give a marketing report credit it has not earned.

**CRM lead reconciliation is the process of connecting records across systems while preserving what each record actually represents.** It is a business-definition problem as much as a technical integration problem.

My lead-data work at ANKURAM IVF involved Meta enquiries, Google Sheets, Bitrix24 and a Windows-based synchronisation worker. Delayed imports and repeat enquiries were part of the operating reality. The lessons below come from that context; the sample records are fictional.

## Separate the person, the enquiry and the opportunity

These three objects often get collapsed into one:

- A **person or contact** represents an identity used for communication.
- An **enquiry** represents a particular request made at a particular time.
- An **opportunity or deal** represents a commercial workflow with its own progression.

One person can make several enquiries. One enquiry may connect to an opportunity, but sharing a contact does not prove that connection. An opportunity may have been created before the campaign being measured.

Imagine a person who enquires in January, does not proceed, and submits a new form in September. Treating the September submission as a duplicate solely because the phone number already exists would erase evidence of renewed intent. Treating an old deal as the result of the September campaign would create a different error.

The identity model must preserve both the continuing relationship and the distinct enquiry events.

## Start with a map of record authority

Before writing matching rules, decide which system is authoritative for each fact.

| Fact | Suggested authority | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Original form submission ID and time | Acquisition source | Identifies the enquiry event |
| Master-row creation | One designated ingestion process | Prevents competing writers from creating duplicates |
| CRM owner and workflow status | CRM | Reflects the operational team's current work |
| Explicit lead-to-deal relationship | CRM relationship record | Provides stronger linkage than a shared phone number |
| Consultation attendance | Approved centre or clinical workflow | Prevents an advertising event from inventing an operational outcome |

This is a starting design, not a rule that every organisation must copy. Some businesses have a different system of record. The important point is to make the choice explicit and stop downstream tools from silently overruling it.

In my project, keeping one owner for new Master rows helped separate ingestion from later enrichment. The worker could then focus on matching and approved updates rather than behaving as another unrestricted record creator.

## Use matching rules that can admit uncertainty

A useful matcher needs more than “match found” and “not found.” I would use states such as confirmed, candidate, ambiguous and pending arrival.

**Confirmed:** a preserved source identifier or an explicit, valid system relationship establishes the link.

**Candidate:** supporting contact details and timing suggest a relationship, but the evidence is insufficient for an irreversible attribution change.

**Ambiguous:** multiple plausible records exist, or strong identifiers disagree.

**Pending arrival:** the source enquiry exists but the expected CRM record may not yet have been imported.

Phone normalisation and email comparison can support candidate discovery. They do not automatically prove that two enquiry events are identical. Shared numbers, recycled numbers, corrected details and family contact patterns all make blind identity assumptions risky.

When evidence conflicts, preserve the records and surface the disagreement. A smaller confirmed match rate is more useful than an impressive number built from guesses.

## Treat delayed imports as a normal state

A synchronisation process may run every few minutes while the CRM receives bulk imports less frequently. During that gap, the same source enquiry can repeatedly appear unmatched.

Creating a fresh CRM record on every pass makes the gap worse. Immediately classifying it as a permanent failure is also misleading.

A more controlled approach is to record when the enquiry was first observed, when matching was last attempted and when the next attempt is due. A defined pending window distinguishes expected delay from a genuine exception. The window should come from observed import behaviour, not an arbitrary promise of “real time.”

For example, a hypothetical worker might revisit unresolved records after a scheduled import completes, then escalate records that remain unmatched beyond the agreed operating window. That is a proposed control, not a claim about the timing of every run in my project.

## Make retries safe without deleting legitimate repetition

Two different forms of repetition need different treatment:

1. The **same event is delivered again** because a request timed out or a job restarted.
2. The **same person makes a new enquiry** and receives a new source event ID.

The first should normally avoid creating another copy of the same action. The second should remain a distinct event.

A stable source event ID is therefore a better starting point for ingestion idempotency than a phone number. AWS explains why retryable operations need a way to recognise repeated requests without confusing them with new intent in its guide to [idempotent APIs](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/).

For updates, the operation identity may also need the target record, action and intended version. Otherwise, a mechanism that correctly blocks duplicate creation could accidentally suppress a later legitimate status change.

## Restrict enrichment and verify what was written

Matching a record does not give a worker unlimited authority to modify it.

I would maintain a field-level write policy: which fields the worker may populate, whether it may only fill blanks, which source wins on disagreement and which fields require human review. A campaign source field and a counsellor's operational status may need different rules.

After an important write, read the permitted fields back from the target system. A successful request response tells you that a request was accepted; readback checks the state on which the next process will depend.

The ANKURAM project record includes selected successful writes and readback, together with stale-status correction. That is specific evidence of particular behaviours. It should not be stretched into a claim that every historical record was reconciled perfectly.

## Measure data reliability separately from business performance

A reconciliation dashboard should answer questions about the integration itself:

- What proportion of source enquiries reached the Master dataset?
- How many have confirmed CRM links, and how many remain ambiguous?
- How old is the oldest unresolved record?
- How many approved writes passed readback?
- Are previously processed records being revisited safely after restarts?

These are different from qualified-lead rate, consultation attendance or revenue.

My portfolio documents a separate historical audit covering **28,122 approved leads with zero reported API errors**. That statement describes processing scope and reported API execution. It does not mean that all records matched, that attribution was complete or that downstream conversion events reached an advertising platform.

Keeping these distinctions visible protects management from treating a technically successful batch as proof of commercial impact.

## Build an exception queue people can resolve

A useful exception record contains the issue category, safe record reference, evidence checked, responsible owner and next review date. It should not copy unnecessary personal or clinical information into a new reporting surface.

Consider three fictional cases:

| Situation | Safe response |
| --- | --- |
| One enquiry links to two plausible CRM leads | Hold attribution; ask the designated reviewer to establish the correct relationship |
| A direct lead-to-deal link conflicts with a contact-only candidate | Preserve both pieces of evidence; investigate the authoritative relationship |
| A source field is populated with a conflicting value | Record the conflict; do not overwrite simply to increase completeness |

Exceptions are part of a reliable system. The goal is to reduce unresolved uncertainty, not hide it behind a single green success indicator.

## Prove readiness with a small acceptance matrix

Before expanding a reconciliation workflow, I would test a new enquiry, a replayed event, a legitimate repeat enquiry, a delayed import, multiple candidate matches, an API timeout and a process restart.

For each case, define the expected records and prohibited changes. “The script completed” is not enough. The evidence should show that the correct relationship was preserved and the wrong relationship was not created.

Only then should more advanced downstream uses be considered. Historical completeness, sustained latency, restart recovery and conversion-platform receipt are separate acceptance questions. In my documented project, several of those remained distinct follow-on items.

Trustworthy attribution starts with trustworthy relationships between records. The most valuable integration may be the one that refuses to manufacture certainty when the evidence is incomplete.

See the [Lead Data Reconciliation and CRM Reliability project](/projects/lead-data-reconciliation-crm-reliability) for the documented implementation context. For the broader management view, read my article on [RevOps dashboard design](/blogs/revops-dashboard-metrics-decisions).
